title: How to Run Cold Email and LinkedIn in One Sequence
summary: How to combine cold email and LinkedIn in one sequence: step order, timing, connected vs not connected branches, and a full 14-day example with copy.
body_markdown:
Most outbound runs on one channel. You send four emails, and if the prospect never sees them, that contact is done. Adding LinkedIn to the same sequence gives each person a second way to notice you, without doubling the noise.


Below: why it works, how to order and space the steps, how to branch on the connection request, and how to stop everything on a reply. There is a full 14-day example you can copy today.


## Why combining channels works


**Familiarity.** A cold email from a stranger reads differently than one from someone whose name showed up in their notifications yesterday. A profile visit or post like costs the prospect nothing, but it makes your email feel less cold.


**More surfaces.** Some people live in their inbox. Others ignore email from unknown senders and actually read LinkedIn messages. If you only use one channel, you only reach one type of person.


**A different inbox.** Email has spam filters, tabs, and an inbox full of vendors. LinkedIn messages land somewhere else entirely. If one channel has a bad week, the other one is unaffected.


What it does not do is make a weak offer work. If your email would not get replies on its own, adding LinkedIn usually just means more people ignore you in more places.


## How to order the steps


A simple rule: **light LinkedIn touches first, the real pitch by email, conversation on LinkedIn.**


1. **Start with a profile visit.** It is the lowest-friction touch there is, and it costs nothing.
2. **Send the first email the same day or the next.** Email carries the actual pitch. It has room for context, it can be forwarded internally, and it is where most people handle work requests.
3. **Send the connection request a day or two after the first email.** By then your name may ring a bell. A request with no note, or a very short one, is a common starting point. A long pitch in the note tends to read as spam. For wording, see these[LinkedIn connection request templates](https://supersend.io/blog/linkedin-connection-request-templates) .
4. **Use LinkedIn messages for conversation, not a second pitch.** Once someone accepts, your message should be short and human, and it should point back to the email instead of repeating it.


Why not lead with the connection request? You can. But a request from a stranger with no context is easy to ignore, while one from the person who just emailed about something specific has a reason to exist.


## Timing between steps


- **Leave 1 to 3 business days between touches.** Close enough that they connect the dots, far enough apart that it does not feel like a pile-on.
- **Never stack two channels on the same day for a "real" touch.** A profile visit on the same day as an email is fine. An email and a LinkedIn message on the same day is too much.
- **Send in their working hours.** Set send windows in the prospect's timezone, and spread LinkedIn actions across the day rather than firing them all at 9:00.
- **Keep LinkedIn volume conservative.** LinkedIn does not publish exact limits. Commonly cited ranges are something like 15 to 25 connection requests a day per account, and many people go lower on new or quiet accounts. LinkedIn's terms also restrict automation, so treat any automated LinkedIn activity as a risk you accept knowingly. More detail in our post on[LinkedIn automation limits and safe pacing](https://supersend.io/blog/linkedin-automation-limits) .


## Connected vs not connected


The connection request is the fork in the road. Some people accept within hours, some after a week, many never.


The cleanest way to handle this is a **wait-until-connected** step with a time limit. The sequence pauses on that contact until they accept or the window runs out (five business days is a reasonable default), then takes one of two paths.


**If they connect:** you now have a second channel for conversation. Send a short thank-you message that references your email, then alternate between channels for the rest of the sequence.


**If they do not connect:** do not chase them on LinkedIn. Skip the LinkedIn messages, keep the remaining emails, and maybe add one more profile visit as a quiet reminder. Withdrawing requests that have sat pending for a few weeks is a common habit worth doing by hand.


In SuperSend, wait-until-connected is its own step in the same sequence as your emails, so you are not checking by hand who accepted before a LinkedIn message goes out.


## How to avoid double-pitching


Double-pitching is when the prospect gets the same pitch in their inbox on Tuesday and in their LinkedIn DMs on Wednesday. It makes you look automated, because you are.


- **Give each step one job.** Email 1 pitches. The connection request asks to connect. The first LinkedIn message starts a conversation. Write the purpose next to every step before you write any copy.
- **Reference, do not repeat.** "I sent you a note by email last week" is fine. Pasting the same three paragraphs is not.
- **Change the angle on later steps.** If email 2 is about saving time, email 3 can be about a risk or a different use case. Same offer, different door.
- **Use one identity.** The person on the LinkedIn account should be the same person signing the emails. Two different names from the same company feels like a campaign, not a person.


## Stop everything on a reply


This is the most important rule in the whole playbook. If someone replies on either channel, every remaining step on both channels should stop.


Nothing burns goodwill faster than replying "not interested" on LinkedIn and getting a cheerful follow-up email two days later.


Things to check before you launch:


- A reply on email stops LinkedIn steps, and a reply on LinkedIn stops email steps. In SuperSend, a reply on either channel stops both, and all replies land in one unified inbox.
- Out-of-office replies are handled the way you want (paused, not treated as a real response).
- Replies that come from somewhere your tool cannot see, like a colleague forwarding your email or a comment on your post, get the contact marked as finished by hand.


## A full 14-day example sequence


Here is a complete sequence that follows everything above. Days are business days from the start.


Day Channel Step Purpose


1 LinkedIn Profile visit Put your name in front of them before anything lands


1 Email Email 1: the pitch One problem, one offer, one question


3 LinkedIn Connection request (no note) Ask to connect once your name has some context


3 to 8 LinkedIn Wait until connected (max 5 days) Decide which branch they go down


4 Email Email 2: same thread, short bump Add one useful detail, not a "just checking in"


6 LinkedIn Like a recent post (skip if none) A light touch with no ask


9 Email Email 3: new angle Different problem or use case, new subject


14 Email Email 4: close the loop Polite last note, door left open


### The branching variant


From the wait-until-connected step on, the sequence splits:


Day If connected If not connected


Day after they accept LinkedIn message 1: thanks, reference the email (nothing, keep waiting until day 8)


9 Email 3: new angle Email 3: new angle


11 LinkedIn message 2: one question, no pitch LinkedIn profile visit


14 Email 4: close the loop Email 4: close the loop


If you want to tune the number of emails and the gaps between them, our guide on[how many follow-ups to send](https://supersend.io/blog/cold-email-follow-up-sequence) goes deeper.


### Example copy


Say you sell software that turns customer onboarding calls into a guided setup flow for SaaS companies.


**Email 1 (day 1)**


> Subject: onboarding at {{company}}
>
>
> Hi {{firstName}},
>
>
> Saw {{company}} is hiring another onboarding specialist. That usually means setup calls are eating a lot of the CS team's week.
>
>
> We help SaaS teams replace the first few setup calls with a guided in-app flow, so new accounts get live without a calendar invite.
>
>
> Worth a 15-minute look, or is onboarding not a priority this quarter?
>
>
> {{senderName}}


**LinkedIn message 1 (after they connect)**


> Thanks for connecting, {{firstName}}. I sent you a short email about onboarding at {{company}}, so I won't repeat it here. If DMs are easier than email, happy to chat here instead. Is onboarding on your list this quarter at all?


**Email 3 (day 9, new angle)**


> Subject: who notices first?
>
>
> Hi {{firstName}},
>
>
> Different question from my last note. When a new account stalls in its first week, who at {{company}} usually notices first, CS or sales?
>
>
> If the answer is "nobody until renewal", that's the gap we close. Happy to show you how in 15 minutes.
>
>
> {{senderName}}


Notice that none of these repeat each other. Each one has a single job, and the LinkedIn message is clearly from the same person who sent the email.


## The short version


- Use LinkedIn for familiarity and conversation, and email for the actual pitch.
- Order it as profile visit, email, connection request, then alternate, with 1 to 3 business days between real touches.
- Branch on the connection request: connected contacts get LinkedIn messages, everyone else gets emails only.
- Give every step one job so you never pitch the same thing twice.
- A reply on either channel stops everything, on both channels.
